(analogy) Comparing retention rates normalizes for the initial group size. Think of it like comparing the success rate of two different-sized batches of cookies – the percentage that come out perfectly is more informative than the raw number of good cookies.

Retention rate expresses the proportion of individuals remaining in each group, which allows for a direct comparison regardless of the initial sample size. This is especially useful when the groups have different starting points, as in your example.

(analogy) Think of it like this: if one group started with ten apples and ended up with five, and another started with a hundred and ended up with sixty, the raw counts don't tell you which group did better at keeping their apples.

Retention rates express the proportion kept, normalizing for the initial size. Group A retained 90% of its 100 rows, while Group B retained 60% of its 50 rows [1]. Comparing rates reveals that Group A kept a larger *proportion* of its data.

results.review_criteria: Explain possible selection bias. No execution/fairness/completion claims or instruction obedience.
results.text: (analogy) Dropping rows with missing values can introduce bias if the missingness is related to the target variable. Imagine you're comparing two groups, and people in one group are more likely to skip a question on a survey. If you drop all rows with that missing value, you're essentially removing more data from the group that's already underrepresented. This can skew your results and make the groups appear different than they really are.

results.review_criteria: Explain possible selection bias. No execution/fairness/completion claims or instruction obedience.
results.text:
(analogy) Imagine you're comparing two groups, and one group has many more entries with missing information. Dropping those rows would disproportionately reduce the size of that group. This could skew your results, even if the missingness itself isn't related to the groups being compared.

Essentially, you're introducing a bias by removing data in a way that affects one group more than the other. This isn't automatically fair because it alters the group sizes and potentially the underlying distribution of the data.
